description: Take product photos that work with AI using just a phone: daylight setup, framing, focus and a quick pre-upload look, so your first results match the real item.
h1: How to Take Product Photos for AI With Just Your Phone
lead: To take product photos for AI, shoot the real item on your phone in window light, fill the frame, and leave filters off so later images still match what you ship.
secondary_keywords: how to photograph products for an online store
summary: Shoot at product height in window light, with filters off and the label readable, then add a few angles and one plain sentence.

sections.h2: How do I do product photography with a phone?
paras: Use the regular camera, rest the phone so it cannot shake, and keep the whole product sharp.

A stack of books or a small tripod, plus the volume button or a two-second timer, stops blur on small print. Fill most of the frame and leave a slim margin on every side. Step closer instead of pinching to zoom.
sections.alt: Adult cleans a plain gray running shoe beside an indirect daylight window.

sections.h2: How do I set product photo lighting at home?
paras: Set the product beside a window in bright, indirect daylight and turn the ceiling lights off.

If sun lands on the table, tape baking paper or a thin white sheet over the glass. Warm room bulbs mixed with daylight shift the color, and that shift follows the product into every later image. A plain board, gray card, or bare wood top is enough background. Wipe dust, peel stickers, and smooth anything soft before you shoot.
sections.alt: Adult hands place a plain gray running shoe on a white board in daylight.

sections.h2: How do I photograph products for an online store?
paras: Hold the phone level with the product, keep every edge inside the frame, and switch portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings off.

Shooting down on a bottle or a box makes it look as if it is tipping backward. Tap the label to lock focus. If white areas look blown out, lower the brightness until the surface texture comes back. Those phone effects change edges and color, and the changes can ride into the new picture.
sections.alt: Plain gray running shoe centered with its full shape and edges in focus.

sections.h2: Which product photo angles should I shoot?
paras: Take a straight front view, then two or three more sides while the setup is still out.

A mug wants the handle side, a look inside, and the mark on the base. A shoe wants the profile, a three-quarter front, and the sole. Lay clothing flat or hang it on a plain door, then add one close frame of the cloth. Upload each side you care about. Do not ask the tool to invent a side it never saw. Those extra stills also give [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) a clearer start.
sections.alt: Adult hands rotate a plain gray running shoe through several source-photo angles.

sections.h2: What should I check before I upload a product photo?
paras: Zoom until you can read the label, then hold the real item next to the screen and compare the color in daylight.

Edges should be crisp, not smeared. Move cups, lids, and anything else out of the frame. Upload the original file, not a screenshot or a picture that passed through a chat app, because those copies are usually compressed. The uploader accepts JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, HEIF, BMP, TIF, and TIFF. The default limit is 32 MB.
sections.alt: Adult hands compare a plain gray running shoe with a blank silhouette card.

sections.h2: How do I describe the scene so the result stays accurate?
paras: Name the product, the surface, and the light in one plain sentence, and leave prices and headlines out.

"A matte black bottle on a gym bench in early light" is useful. "Make it look premium" is not. Add the price later in your own editor, where the spelling stays yours. From this photo you can open the [AI product photo generator](page:photo-hub) for other looks, or make [AI lifestyle product photos](page:lifestyle-photos) when the listing needs a setting.

faq.q: How do I photograph a shiny product?
faq.a: Shoot near a window and stand a white card on the far side so light fills the shadows. Turn the item until the window's reflection sits on an edge, not across the label. Skip the flash, which leaves a hard white spot.

faq.q: Does the photo need a white background first?
faq.a: No. A plain, uncluttered background is enough. Make a white version afterward if a marketplace asks for one.

faq.q: Can the photo include another brand's logo?
faq.a: Leave it out. Requests built around logos you do not own, or around famous people, may be refused. Crop them away or reshoot with only your product in frame.

faq.q: What if the color looks wrong on my phone?
faq.a: Compare the screen with the real item in daylight before you upload. If the phone turned it yellow or gray, reshoot with the ceiling lights off.

faq.q: How many credits does one product photo use?
faq.a: One image uses 24 credits. You see that cost before the job starts, and a failed job returns the credits.

faq.q: Should I use portrait mode for a product?
faq.a: No. Stay on the regular lens with portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings off so the edges and colors stay honest.
